title: Using the Godfather to Help with Belonging
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart describes a recurring classroom ritual he uses when returning the year's first test results: introducing students to a Godfather line, it's not personal, it's business, as shorthand for interpreting test scores as information rather than as judgment on their identity. He diagnoses the underlying problem directly through his Five Key Beliefs framework, arguing that both an I'm stupid and an I'm smart reading of a test score are motivational liabilities, since the first strengthens a fixed mindset and undercuts Effort and Belonging, while the second makes identity contingent on performance and turns every subsequent test into a threat. His fix isn't a one-time speech but a repeated framing students hear all year, treating feedback, including summative results, as data that guides further learning rather than as a verdict on who they are. He closes by generalizing the technique: whatever memorable framing a teacher uses, students need to hear the point again and again, not just once at the start of the year.
points: Stuart's Godfather framing gives students a repeatable, memorable phrase for reinterpreting test scores as information rather than identity-defining judgment.

He treats both an "I'm stupid" and an "I'm smart" self-narrative as motivational liabilities, arguing the smart narrative is just as harmful because it makes future Effort feel unnecessary and every test a threat to self-image.
His broader point is that reframing needs constant repetition, not a single opening speech, since students will default back to taking scores personally without ongoing reinforcement.
quotes: Many students take their test results personally. They see a score, and they think, oh, I'm stupid, or, oh, I'm smart.
Whether you summarize a test score into I'm stupid or I'm smart, the result is the same: the test result stops teaching you. Instead, it judges you, giving you a summary of who you are.
The most productive and lighthearted of learners are those who see test results as information, not as judgment.
When kids infer from test results that they are smart or stupid, they're internalizing an anti-Effort belief. To put it in a buzzwordier way, they are in that moment strengthening a fixed mindset.

The I'm smart interpretation means that my identity as a learner is based on my performance on tests. In this situation, each test becomes a threat to one's sense of self, and as a result tests get toxically stressful.

What I'm trying to do, all year long, is help students interpret feedback, including summative test results, as information that guides their learning. It's about the business we are about in school: learning.
